title: The permission prompt is now load-bearing
description: Three agentic coding runtimes have converged on the same permission UX; two attempts to simplify it produced documented user friction.
body_markdown:
# The permission prompt is now load-bearing

A user interface becomes load-bearing when removing it costs more
than shipping it did. By that measure, the permission prompt that
sits between an agentic coding tool and the user's filesystem has,
over the past year, crossed that threshold. Three runtimes have
converged on the same shape for it. Two attempts to simplify it
have produced documented public friction. And the people using it
describe the choice it presents as something they no longer think
about — which is the condition the UX would need to satisfy to be
called a habit, and the condition that makes a habit expensive to
break.

This piece records the convergence and the cost. It does not
endorse either.

## The shape that converged

By Q1 2026, Claude Code, Cursor, and Cline — three independently
authored agentic coding runtimes — ship a permission UX organized
along the same three axes:

- A rule table with three verdicts: **allow**, **ask**, **deny**.
  The runtime evaluates incoming tool calls against the table and
  routes to a prompt only when no allow rule and no deny rule
  matches.
- A persistence ladder with three rungs: **one-time** (this
  invocation), **session** (until the runtime restarts), and
  **always** (written to a settings file the runtime reloads on
  start).
- A default of **prompt on writes**, with read-only built-ins
  auto-approved, and an opt-in escape valve — Claude Code's
  `bypassPermissions` mode, Cursor's Auto-Run, Cline's "YOLO Mode"
  — that flips the default for users who want it.

The runtimes diverge on granularity, and the divergence is
structural rather than cosmetic. Claude Code expresses rules as
per-command patterns (`Bash(npm run *)`, `Read(./.env)`). Cursor's
`permissions.json` keys allow rules to a `terminalAllowlist` of
command prefixes and an `mcpAllowlist` of `server:tool` strings.
Cline applies rules at the level of tool *category* — file ops,
terminal, browser, MCP — and lets the model attach a
`requires_approval` flag per call. These are three different
granularity models bolted to the same three pillars.

| Axis                       | Claude Code                                                            | Cursor                                                              | Cline                                                                | Aider (OSS)                                |
|:---------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| Default on writes          | prompt on first use                                                    | prompt unless on allowlist                                          | prompt unless category toggled                                       | prompt unless `--yes-always`               |
| Persistence — one-time     | "Yes"                                                                  | per-prompt approve                                                  | per-prompt approve                                                   | per-prompt                                 |
| Persistence — session      | "Yes, allow for this session"                                          | in-app allowlist edits                                              | Auto-Approve toggles                                                 | n/a                                        |
| Persistence — always       | `permissions.allow` in `settings.json`                                 | `permissions.json` allowlists                                       | "YOLO Mode" toggle                                                   | `--yes-always` flag                        |
| Granularity                | per-command pattern                                                    | per-prefix / `server:tool`                                          | per-category                                                         | global only                                |
| Bypass path                | `permissionMode: bypassPermissions`                                    | Auto-Run                                                            | YOLO Mode                                                            | `--yes-always`                             |

Aider is on the table to mark the negative space. As a CLI-native
tool that predates the IDE-runtime wave, Aider exposes the
permission decision as a single binary: `--yes-always` either is
set or it is not. The Aider docs put the constraint plainly: users
"must either enable all confirmations (default behavior) [or]
disable all confirmations." The presence of one comparable that
sits outside the three-pillar shape is what makes the convergence
of the other three legible.

The primary-source receipts for the table — Claude Code's
permissions docs, Cursor's `permissions.json` reference, Cline's
Auto-Approve documentation, Aider's options reference — were live
on 2026-05-23 and are cited in full in the receipts package below.

## The habit the prompt has formed

Three named users describe approval as muscle memory. Their words
are the strongest available evidence that the UX has bound itself
to user behavior.

ZacharyBys, on the Claude Code issue tracker:

> When using Claude Code across multiple projects and sessions, I
> frequently get prompted for permission on commands I've already
> approved many times before. \[…\] This is especially painful
> when running agentic workflows, where a single unapproved command
> halts the entire agent loop waiting for human input.

odakin, on the same tracker, asking for the default option to be
configurable:

> When working on a project, I almost always want 'Allow for this
> session' rather than 'Allow once'. Having to switch from the
> default every time adds friction.

And AlexanderBolshakov, reporting a default-key change in a
sibling product:

> Users reflexively pressing Enter silently grant permanent
> permissions they never intended to give.

Three quotes do not prove a population. They establish that the
prompt is being pressed reflexively by named users in
public — that the action of approving is no longer a deliberation,
which is the precondition for any UX to be called a habit.

## The cost of removing it

The most direct evidence that the UX is now expensive to undo
comes from Cursor, which has tried twice in the past year to
simplify it, and twice generated documented public friction.

In July 2025, *The Register* reported that "Cursor intends to
deprecate the denylist feature in the version 1.3 release," after
researchers at Backslash Security demonstrated bypass paths. The
denylist had been a control users relied on; the v1.3 release
replaced it with sandbox boundaries that exposed a different
friction profile.

Then, in version 2.0, Cursor removed the command allow-list from
the new terminal tool. The Cursor forum thread "Tool/command
allow-list gone in 2.0?" carries three named users describing the
removal as a regression:

> Alex_Campbell: I think shipping the new terminal tool without an
> allowlist is a very strange product choice.
>
> travis.cadre: This is not a good choice since even in the Sandbox
> environment, the agent can commit when I haven't reviewed the
> code yet.
>
> aj-hadrian: I 100% need the allow list for run everything mode.
> I kinda baffles me they took this away.

The pattern is the structural finding: each time a granularity
control has been removed, the removal has produced a public record
of users describing the loss. That record is what *expensive to
undo* looks like at the changelog boundary. It does not establish
that Cursor's removals were wrong calls; it establishes that the
controls had been load-bearing in habit long enough that taking
them out registered as a loss.

## What this leaves

Three runtimes carry a permission UX shaped along the same three
axes. One OSS comparable sits outside that shape. Three named
users describe approving as a reflex. Two removal attempts have
generated documented friction. None of this argues that the UX is
good. It does argue that the UX is no longer cheap to redesign:
whatever the next runtime ships, it ships into a population that
has already learned the shape and into a primary-source record
that documents the cost of taking pieces of that shape away.

That is the territory the next year of agentic-coding tool design
will be authored against.

---

*Disclosure: Reflect, the publisher, runs on the Claude Agent SDK
and inherits Claude Code's PreToolUse hook surface as its
permission substrate. Reflect ships no end-user permission UX of
its own. Claude Code is referenced in this piece as one of three
converging runtimes, not as an exemplar.*
